title: After a year of nights and weekends, my co-op ape delivery game is almost here (made with a lot of AI help, and a lot of not-AI)
author: nosark
selftext:
I've been lurking here for a long time, reading about other people's games and their wins and headaches with AI tools. It's helped me a ton, so I wanted to finally share mine.

**Ape Express** is a co-op delivery adventure for 1–4 players. You and your crew of apes drive one battered red pickup across a valley of jungle roads, river crossings, axle-deep swamp mud, snowy mountain passes and crystal caves. Your cargo is often fragile, toxic, and sometimes alive.

# A bit of background

I made my first game when I was 12. It was a truly horrible galaxy shooter in Visual Basic, and I was hooked for life. I went on to become a professional programmer, but I always wanted to make a real game of my own. Ape Express is that game, and it's been a labor of love for about a year.

# Some of the tools

* **Claude** for code. It was my pair programmer all the way through
* **Meshy** for 3D models. 
* **Nano Banana** for concept art and loading screens
* **Blender** and **GIMP** for fixing, editing and making everything else

# The music

It was important to me that the music is not AI. I hired a composer, **Mayra Gandra**, to write and perform an original soundtrack. Every area of the valley has its own music, and it's one of my favorite parts of the game. She's awesome, so please go check out her work on her [Instagram](http://instagram.com/mayragandramusic) and her [Youtube](https://www.youtube.com/@SoundScapeFantasy) channel.

# What else AI didn't do

This is the part I really wanted to write about. AI tools made this game possible for one person, but they did not make the game. A lot of my time went into:

* **Multiplayer** \- Making physics-heavy co-op feel good over a real network connection means prediction, rollback and a lot of debugging. AI can help write that code, but someone has to understand why the truck is teleporting on your friend's screen. I used Purrnet and Purrdiction. If any of you are familiar with Bobsi on Youtube, him and Valentin are invaluable helpers on their discord channel.
* **Fixing generated models** \- Meshy gets you surprisingly far, but I spent many hours in Blender repairing normals, fixing UVs, removing floating geometry and rigging things so they actually move right. 
* **Level design, dialogue, and feel** \- Where the road goes, how steep a hill is, whether a puzzle is fun or just annoying. What the NPCs say to you. That's playtesting, iterating and throwing away things that didn't work. I did around 500 hours of testing with 3 very patient friends.
* **Performance** \- Profiling and optimizing so it runs on my friend's older PC, not just mine.
* **Holding it all together** \- Every system has to work with every other system. That's still the job.  As a programmer, my honest take is that AI made me much faster, but every hard problem was still mine to solve.

# Where it's at

Ape Express launches on Steam on January 12, 2027, and there's a free demo out now if you want to try the first couple checkpoints with your band of friends: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/2271240/Ape\_Express/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2271240/Ape_Express/)

If you play it, I'd genuinely love your feedback. I'm also happy to answer questions about the workflow, the tools, or what worked and what didn't.

**Thanks for being such a good corner of the internet for this stuff.**
